title: Tenka Smart Contract Security Audit
protocolOverview: Tenka is a tokenized private-credit platform that lets investors access off-chain deals through on-chain vaults. A MasterVault pools stablecoin liquidity and allocates it to per-deal FundingVaults, which in turn take positions in tranche-based DealVaults representing individual raises. Pricing is driven by an Oracle publishing periodic NAV checkpoints, primary allocation runs through a Bookbuild auction, and all primary and secondary trading is KYC-gated and executed through a central MatchingEngine. An MMF integration (via an Agora/Uniswap V3 helper) puts idle FundingVault liquidity to work between raises.
auditScope: This audit covers 12 smart contracts and the mainnet deployment script across the DealVault, MasterVault/FundingVault, MatchingEngine, Oracle, and Bookbuild modules, reviewed over 9 days from September 1 to September 11, 2026.
overallAssessment: Tenka is a well-built, thoughtfully engineered codebase backed by a responsive and knowledgeable team. Findings from this review concentrated in the interactions between independently reasonable subsystems: Oracle timing versus distributions, rounding at settlement boundaries, and the trust boundary between factory-created vaults and the contracts that rely on them, rather than in any single component. The team engaged closely throughout, confirmed intended behavior quickly, and shipped fixes with regression tests for nearly every finding before this report was finalized. The protocol is intentionally centralized around a small set of operator and strategic roles that control matching, NAV publication, and vault creation. This is a deliberate design choice for a compliance-gated private-credit product, and it meaningfully reduces the on-chain attack surface compared to a permissionless design, but it also means the security of user funds ultimately depends on the operational security and honesty of those privileged roles, as reflected in the operator-trust findings in this report.

│   ├── DealVaultBookbuild.sol
│   └── Queue.sol

    ├── TenkaFundingFactory.sol

    ├── MMFManager.sol
    └── AgoraHelper.sol

evaluations.description: Role checks within individual contracts were sound, but the boundary between privileged roles and the contracts that trust them had gaps: a routine operator role could create attacker-owned vaults that downstream contracts trusted automatically, and KYC status was not always re-checked at the point where value actually moved (revoked sellers, non-KYC transfer recipients). All of these were fixed by separating factory authority onto timelocks/multisigs and adding payer-side KYC checks.

Core accounting was correct, but several settlement paths did not handle boundary conditions: zero-output rounding in partial order fills, negative MMF returns underflowing cancellation math, and a division-by-zero on zero-NAV turbo claims. These were rounding and edge-case gaps rather than fundamental pricing errors, and most were remediated with explicit checks.

The protocol composes several independently reasonable subsystems (Oracle NAV publication, Bookbuild auctions, tranche accounting, an MMF yield strategy) whose cross-contract timing assumptions were not always enforced on-chain. Most findings in this report are ordering/sequencing issues at these seams rather than bugs within a single contract, which is typical of a system this size and was mitigated through a mix of code changes and documented operational procedure.

The codebase builds on well-established primitives (OpenZeppelin access control/ERC standards, Uniswap V3 for the MMF swap path) and uses them correctly in the vast majority of cases. The one notable gap, an unrestricted public swap() combined with unvalidated partial-fill deltas in the Uniswap V3 helper, was fixed by sweeping residual balances after each swap.

Tenka is intentionally centralized: NAV publication, order matching, and vault creation are controlled by a small set of operator and strategic roles rather than being permissionless. This is a reasonable trade-off for a KYC-gated private-credit product and reduces on-chain attack surface, but it concentrates trust in those roles, as illustrated by the rogue-vault-creation and compromised-operator round-trip findings. Post-audit changes moved factory and vault-creation authority behind timelocks/multisigs, which meaningfully tightens this without removing the underlying centralization.

Inline documentation of invariants (e.g. matching token decimals across a DealVault) was present and accurate where it existed, and the team was consistently able to confirm intended behavior quickly and precisely during the review, indicating strong internal understanding of the system's design.

The existing test suite was a solid baseline, and the team was receptive to auditor-supplied proof-of-concept tests, several of which were incorporated directly. Nearly every fix shipped during the review was accompanied by new regression tests covering the specific scenario found, reflecting a healthy testing culture.

issues.title: `DealVault` Does Not Enforce Matching Token Decimals
Negative MMF returns can lock bookbuild bids and subscribed rounds
issues.body:
`DealVaultBookbuild` records each bid's original asset amount separately from the ERC-4626 shares received from the configured `MmfVault`. Several settlement paths assume those shares can never become worth less than the original bid. If the staging vault realizes a loss, bidders may be unable to cancel while the raise is open, and a sufficiently subscribed round can become stuck in `PROCESSING` without an available refund transition.

#### Technical Details

During cancellation, `_processCancelCommit()` calculates the MMF yield as:

```solidity
uint256 mmfPenalty = (currentAssetValue - originalBidAmount) * bidAmount / originalBidAmount;
```

If `previewRedeem(node.amount) < originalBidAmount`, the subtraction underflows and `cancelCommit()` reverts.

The state transition has the same underlying accounting mismatch. `advanceState()` selects `PROCESSING` by comparing the nominal `totalBidAmount` against `targetRaiseAmount`; it does not consider the current redeemable value of the staging-vault shares. `processBids()` then redeems the shares but continues to use the recorded gross bid:

```solidity
uint256 assets = IERC4626(stagingVault).redeem(node.amount, address(this), address(this));
_stakeFor(_vault, _tranche, node.user, postPremiumAmount);
feesCollected[asset] += bidAmount - postPremiumAmount;
IERC20(asset).safeTransfer(node.user, assets - bidAmount);
```

For a zero-premium winning bid, staking the original amount fails because the bookbuild received fewer assets. For a premium bid whose loss can still be covered by the premium, `assets - bidAmount` instead underflows. The transaction reverts and restores the dequeued node and redeemed shares. Because cancellations require `RAISING` or `RERAISING` and refunds require `REFUNDING`, there is no built-in path out of `PROCESSING` after this failure.

This condition can arise through the intended MMF flow. `AgoraHelper` accepts up to two basis points of negative swap slippage while `getAssetFromShares()` values the received MMF token at 1:1. Consequently, swapping the staging asset into and back out of the MMF token can reduce `MmfVault.totalAssets()` while its ERC-4626 share supply remains unchanged.

A proof of concept modeled a decrease in `MmfVault` assets after a fully subscribed bid. The bidder's cancellation reverted with arithmetic panic `0x11`; after `advanceState()`, `processBids()` reverted due to insufficient assets; the round remained in `PROCESSING`, the queue was unchanged, and `processRefunds()` reverted with `ErrNotRefunding`.

#### Impact

Low.

#### Recommendation

Handle negative MMF returns explicitly. Use a saturating calculation for positive yield instead of subtracting the original bid unconditionally. Before or during processing, compare redeemable assets with the obligations represented by the bid and define how losses are allocated among the stake, premium, and refund.

If the realized assets cannot support the required allocation, provide a controlled transition from `PROCESSING` to a loss-adjusted refund state. Consider tracking the ERC-4626 shares associated with each round so `advanceState()` can evaluate current redeemable value rather than nominal bid accounting alone.


#### Developer Response

Acknowledged, won't fix.

issues.title: Revoked KYC holders can liquidate DealVault positions through the MatchingEngine
issues.body:
The MatchingEngine validates the KYC status of each order's `receiver`, but it does not validate the DealVault seller identified by the ask order's `payer`. A holder whose KYC token has been frozen or revoked can therefore continue controlling and liquidating the position by directing the sale proceeds to another KYC address.

#### Technical Details

Both posting and secondary-market matching check only the receiver:

```solidity
// MatchingEngine.postOrder()
_isKYC(_signedOrder.order.receiver);

// MatchingEngine.matchOrders()
_isKYC(_bidMatch.signedOrder.order.receiver);
_isKYC(_askMatch.signedOrder.order.receiver);
```

For a DealVault ask, however, settlement transfers shares directly from `ask.payer`, not from `ask.receiver`:

```solidity
DealVault(_bidOrder.instrument).transferDeal(
    _askOrder.payer,
    _bidOrder.receiver,
    uint96(_bidOrder.trancheId),
    _instrumentAmount - instrumentFee
);
```

`DealVault.transferDeal()` authorizes the MatchingEngine as the caller but does not validate the current KYC status of `_from`. Consequently, the following path succeeds through the normal `PRE_WINDOW` flow:

1. A KYC-approved seller acquires DealVault shares.
2. The seller's KYC token is subsequently frozen or revoked, for example after the wallet is reported compromised.
3. The old wallet posts or signs an ask with itself as `payer` and another KYC address as `receiver`.
4. A normal KYC and BLP-whitelisted buyer posts a crossing bid.
5. The orders are matched because both receivers pass KYC validation.
6. The DealVault shares leave the revoked wallet and the stablecoin proceeds are sent to the seller-selected KYC receiver.

#### Impact

Medium. KYC revocation is intended to prevent the revoked holder from continuing to control or liquidate its DealVault position. Because the seller's KYC status is not checked, the revoked wallet can nevertheless dispose of its entire position through the ordinary secondary-market path, potentially affecting its full value without malicious operator behavior. This defeats both compromised-wallet recovery and compliance-driven asset restrictions, while allowing the proceeds to be redirected to another KYC address. Exploitation does, however, require access to a KYC proceeds receiver and sufficient matching liquidity.

#### Recommendation

In the paired secondary-market branch of `MatchingEngine.matchOrders()`, validate the ask payer after determining whether the instrument is a MasterVault:

```solidity
if (!isMasterVault) {
    _isKYC(_askMatch.signedOrder.order.payer);
}
```

Performing this check during matching ensures that a DealVault ask cannot execute if the seller's KYC is revoked after the order was posted, while preserving the existing payer/receiver separation for purchases and MasterVault orders.

#### Developer Response

Mitigated in [PR #320](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/pull/320), commit [7eb34298](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/7eb34298e865922e14ceefcedec5fb78216c307d). DealVault secondary settlement now checks the ask payer’s current KYC, preventing revoked or frozen sellers from routing proceeds to another eligible receiver. Tests cover signed orders, revocation after posting, and valid payer/receiver separation. MasterVault behaviour remains unchanged.

issues.title: Routine operator can create trusted rogue vaults and drain funds
issues.body:
The mainnet deployment gives the routine `operator` enough authority to create attacker-owned vaults that the protocol immediately trusts. A malicious authorized operator can use either factory boundary to drain protocol assets:

1. create a rogue FundingVault and drain MasterVault assets through a malicious MMF helper; or
2. create a rogue DealVault whose owner confiscates and repeatedly resells one legitimately backed FundingVault position.

Both paths arise because a factory operator can choose the new vault's owner and factory registration is sufficient for downstream contracts to trust that vault.

#### Technical details

The deployment grants the same routine address roles across both paths:

```solidity
tenkaFundingFactory.grantRole(operator, OPERATOR_ROLE, true);
masterVault.grantRole(operator, OPERATOR_ROLE, true);

dealVaultFactory.grantRole(operator, OPERATOR_ROLE, true);
matchingEngine.grantRole(operator, OPERATOR_ROLE, true);
fundingVault.grantRole(operator, OPERATOR_ROLE, true);
```

Transferring factory and vault ownership to timelocks does not revoke these operator grants.

##### Path 1: rogue FundingVault drains the MasterVault

`TenkaFundingFactory.createVault()` lets a factory operator choose the new FundingVault's owner. It also registers the child, so `MasterVault.allocateFunds()` accepts it as a valid destination.

The operator can:

1. create a registered FundingVault with an attacker-controlled owner;
2. use that ownership to grant child-local roles and configure a malicious MMF helper;
3. allocate MasterVault assets to the child; and
4. process an MMF request that executes the helper with `delegatecall` and transfers the allocated assets out.

The original PoC transferred 500,000 USDC from a MasterVault holding 1,000,000 USDC. Revoking only the routine operator's `TenkaFundingFactory` role stopped this path.

##### Path 2: rogue DealVault owner recycles one backed position

`DealVaultFactory.createVault()` also lets its operator choose any owner and immediately registers the child. After the legitimate FundingVault allocates 100,000 USDC to that child, it receives 100,000 legitimately backed shares.

However, `DealVault.transferDeal()` lets the child owner move shares out of any holder without that holder's approval. The attack is therefore:

1. create a registered DealVault owned by a colluding KYC account;
2. allocate 100,000 USDC from the legitimate FundingVault to establish a fully backed position;
3. have the child owner confiscate those shares from the FundingVault;
4. sell the same shares back to the FundingVault at truthful par; and
5. repeat the confiscate-and-resell cycle nine times during one ordinary settlement window.

The PoC gives the malicious operator no Oracle role. A separate honest Oracle publishes the truthful zero off-chain clean NAV for the fresh OPEN deal; the conversion includes the 100,000 USDC of on-chain raised capital. The FundingVault uses zero price spread, needs no Backstop LP status, and uses no approved receiver path. The colluder supplies no USDC.

After nine par matches, the FundingVault has spent its entire 900,000-USDC idle balance. The colluder receives 899,100 USDC after fees, while the FundingVault retains only the original 100,000-USDC-backed position. The attack needs no virtual mint or child strategic role. Removing the child owner's third-party transfer authority makes the unchanged exploit revert, and revoking only the routine operator's `DealVaultFactory` role prevents creation of the rogue child.

An earlier proof also reached the same loss by letting the rogue child owner self-grant strategic authority and mint unbacked inventory, but that additional authority is unnecessary.

#### Affected code

- `packages/smart-contracts/script/deploy.mainnet.s.sol`: routine operator-role grants
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MasterVault/TenkaFundingFactory.sol`: arbitrary child ownership and automatic registration
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/DealVault/DealVaultFactory.sol`: arbitrary child ownership and automatic registration
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/DealVault/DealVault.sol`: owner transfer authority over third-party holders
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MasterVault/MasterVault.sol`: trusts every registered FundingVault
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MasterVault/FundingVault.sol`: trusts every registered DealVault and posts the par bids
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MasterVault/MMFManager.sol`: helper configuration and request processing
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MatchingEngine.sol`: routine execution of queued FundingVault orders

#### Impact

Medium. A malicious authorized routine operator can cause direct, permanent loss from either the MasterVault or FundingVault. The demonstrated DealVault branch can consume the FundingVault's full idle USDC balance in one ordinary settlement window without false Oracle data, adverse pricing, virtual issuance, an approved receiver, or attacker capital. The required operator authority lowers likelihood despite the potentially large loss.

#### Recommendation

Remove routine factory authority wherever vault creation is intended to require independent approval. Keep both FundingVault and DealVault creation under the intended timelocked multisig or admin Safe, revoke any existing routine grants, and add deployment tests that fail when a routine operator can create attacker-owned trusted vaults.

Do not treat factory registration alone as investment approval. Require an independent allowlist before a MasterVault or FundingVault can allocate to or trade against a newly registered child.

Remove a DealVault owner's ability to transfer shares from arbitrary third-party holders. If a recovery transfer is required, restrict it to separately authorized governance with explicit holder consent and an auditable reason.

#### Developer response

Mitigated through deployment authority separation in [PR #320](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/pull/320), commit [85beebc9](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/85beebc91c65c47212aea551767c12e435a5c98c). FundingVault creation is assigned to the multisig and DealVault creation to the one-day timelock, rather than the routine operator. Temporary deployer roles are revoked and canonical FundingVault ownership is transferred to the multisig.

Commit [333e6665](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/333e6665599c80d77dfc324b63c3800abe636b1c) adds handoff assertions. This mitigation does not introduce an investment allowlist or remove DealVault owner recovery-transfer authority.

issues.title: Compromised operator can drain FundingVault assets through max-spread round trips
Unbound virtual mint and Oracle updates can misprice Bookbuild allocations
Sparse tick scanning can require 101 refund transactions
Partial principal return can be sold again before the Oracle resets dirty NAV
issues.body:
`DealVault.updateYield()` credits a partial principal return to the existing holders without updating the Oracle or blocking secondary settlement. Until the next Oracle update, `convertToAssets()` and the MatchingEngine continue pricing the shares using the previous dirty NAV. A seller can keep the distributed principal and sell the remaining shares as though that principal were still part of the position.

#### Technical details

The project team confirmed that each tranche's Oracle feed contains dirty NAV and that the accumulated portion resets after a distribution. They also confirmed that the intended sequence is to update the Oracle before distributing principal. The code-freeze contracts do not enforce that sequence. The Oracle update, principal distribution, and secondary match are separate transactions, with no pending-distribution flag or checkpoint preventing settlement between them.

Example exploit:

1. Creates a tranche with one million shares and a $1 million dirty NAV.
2. Distributes $400,000 of principal to the existing holder.
3. Sells 240,000 shares before publishing the lower ex-distribution NAV.
4. The MatchingEngine charges the buyer $240,000 because the old $1 million NAV remains active.
5. Those shares represent only $144,000 of the remaining $600,000 principal, leaving the buyer with a $96,000 loss.
6. The seller retains the previously credited $400,000 principal return.

The control publishes the $600,000 ex-distribution NAV before matching. The same 240,000 shares then cost $144,000 and the loss disappears.


#### Affected Code

- `packages/smart-contracts/src/DealVault/DealVault.sol`: `updateYield()`, `convertToAssets()`, `transferDeal()`
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/MatchingEngine.sol`: secondary-order settlement
- `packages/smart-contracts/src/Oracle.sol`: tranche dirty-NAV publication

#### Impact

A buyer can pay for principal that has already been distributed to the seller. The demonstrated scenario causes a $96,000 loss on a $240,000 purchase.

#### Recommendation

Block secondary settlement and new allocations after a principal or yield distribution until a newer Oracle checkpoint clears the pending valuation change. The contracts should enforce this relationship rather than relying only on transaction ordering by the operator.


#### Developer Response

Acknowledged and accepted. NAV updates and yield/principal distributions will be coordinated within our weekly operational cycle. We will suspend matching for affected DealVaults during any gap between the NAV adjustment and the corresponding distribution, including payment delays. Trading will resume only once both are consistent. This restriction will be enforced operationally by our matching operators; no on-chain change is planned.

issues.title: MasterVault shares can be transferred to and liquidated by non-KYC addresses
issues.body:
`MasterVault` inherits unrestricted ERC-20 transfer functions, while its transfer hook enforces only the blacklist. Consequently, a KYC-approved holder can transfer shares directly to an address that has never received a KYC token, bypassing the `MatchingEngine` receiver check. The non-KYC holder can subsequently redeem the shares by directing the proceeds to another KYC-approved address.

#### Technical Details

`BaseVault._update()` is the only restriction applied to share transfers:

```solidity
function _update(address _from, address _to, uint256 _value) internal virtual override {
    _checkBlacklisted(_from);
    _checkBlacklisted(_to);
    super._update(_from, _to, _value);
}
```

No KYC check is performed. Direct `transfer`, `transferFrom`, and ERC-3009 authorized transfers can therefore place MasterVault shares with any non-blacklisted address without going through the `MatchingEngine`.

During primary redemption, `_checkOneWayOrder()` validates only the signed order's `receiver`:

```solidity
_isKYC(_matchingOrder.signedOrder.order.receiver);
```

It does not validate the ask `payer`. `_reduceTokenBalance()` can therefore pull shares from a non-KYC payer into the `MatchingEngine`; the transfer succeeds because `BaseVault` only checks the blacklist, and `MasterVault.redeem()` then burns those shares and sends the redemption assets to the KYC-approved receiver.

An end-to-end sequence is:

1. Alice acquires MasterVault shares while KYC-approved.
2. Alice calls `MasterVault.transfer(bob, shares)`, where Bob has no KYC token. The transfer succeeds.
3. Bob approves the `MatchingEngine` and signs a primary redemption ask with Bob as `payer` and a KYC-approved address as `receiver`.
4. An operator settles the order normally. Bob's shares are pulled and redeemed, and the nominated KYC receiver receives the assets.

The proof of concept in `test/audit/MasterVaultNonKycTransfer.t.sol` demonstrates a non-KYC address receiving and liquidating 100,000 MasterVault shares through this path.

#### Impact

Low. A KYC holder can transfer the full economic exposure represented by its MasterVault shares to a non-KYC party without privileged cooperation or use of the controlled secondary market. The non-KYC holder can then liquidate the position through an ordinary operator-executed redemption by selecting a KYC proceeds receiver. This defeats KYC eligibility and revocation controls and permits OTC ownership changes outside the `MatchingEngine`'s fee and market controls. However, no direct third-party theft occurs, and on-protocol liquidation requires access to a KYC-approved receiver.

#### Recommendation

Enforce current KYC status for ordinary MasterVault share senders and recipients in the transfer hook, while explicitly exempting minting, burning, and any protocol custody contracts that must hold shares. Alternatively, disable direct ERC-20 transfers and require all ownership changes to use the controlled `MatchingEngine` flow.

Independently recheck the MasterVault ask payer's KYC status at execution time for primary redemptions and secondary sales. Execution-time validation is necessary because KYC can be revoked after an order is posted or its shares are escrowed.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged and accepted. Intent to allow non-kyc users to hold mastervault shares is to allow potential defi integrations in the future.

issues.title: Reservation replacement can authorize two allocations
issues.body:
`reserveFor()` overwrites a user's existing reservation without checking whether it was consumed while the replacement transaction was pending. A user can therefore front-run a reservation update, consume the old allocation, and then consume the replacement after the operator's transaction executes.

#### Technical Details

`takeReservation()` reads and clears the current reservation before funding the corresponding DealVault stake:

```solidity
uint256 amount = reservedFor[_vault][_tranche][msg.sender];
reservedFor[_vault][_tranche][msg.sender] = 0;
// transfer funds and stake
```

Meanwhile, `reserveFor()` unconditionally writes the new value:

```solidity
reservedFor[_vault][_tranche][_user] = _amount;
```

If an operator broadcasts a transaction replacing an existing reservation, the reserved user can consume the old value first. The pending update then writes the new value into the cleared slot, allowing the user to fund both allocations.

#### Impact

Low. The user can exceed the allocation intended by the strategic operator, but must fully fund both stakes. The DealVault remains backed, so the consequence is limited to bypassing allocation policy rather than causing insolvency or direct loss.

#### Recommendation

Require reservation updates to include the expected current value and revert if it has changed. Alternatively, clear the old reservation in a confirmed transaction before creating the replacement.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged and accepted. Partners would have access to reservations. Very unlikely that a partner is malicious for more shares of a DealVault.

issues.title: Partial Agora swaps leave vault funds exposed through the public swap function
Zero-NAV turbo claims revert on yield-only distributions
issues.body:
`DealVault.claim(0)` always calculates how many turbo shares to burn after processing a claim. When both the tranche's clean NAV and the claimable principal are zero, this calculation divides by zero and prevents a FundingVault from collecting an otherwise valid yield-only distribution.

#### Technical Details

After `_claim()` determines and transfers the user's yield and principal, tranche-zero claims invoke `_processTurboSharesBurn()`:

```solidity
(uint256 yield, uint256 primitive) = _claim(msg.sender, _trancheMask);
if (_trancheMask == 0) _processTurboSharesBurn(msg.sender, primitive);
```

The burn calculation uses the sum of clean NAV and claimed principal as its denominator:

```solidity
uint256 cleanNav = _getNonStaleCleanNav(0);
uint256 previousCleanNav = cleanNav + _primitive;
uint256 sharesToBurn = balanceOf(_user, 0) * _primitive / previousCleanNav;
```

The oracle accepts a zero tranche NAV, and `updateYield()` permits a positive yield distribution with zero principal. In that state, `cleanNav == 0` and `_primitive == 0`, causing a division-by-zero panic. The revert rolls back the preceding yield transfer and claim accounting.

The FundingVault cannot bypass this path: its claim function calls `DealVault.claim(0)`, while the operator-assisted `claimFor()` and `claimBatch()` functions reject tranche zero.

#### Impact

Low. A FundingVault cannot collect funded yield from a zero-NAV turbo position until principal or NAV becomes nonzero, or the DealVault is finalized. The affected value may be meaningful, but the required zero-NAV plus yield-only state is expected to be uncommon.

#### Recommendation

Return early from `_processTurboSharesBurn()` when `_primitive == 0`, after validating the turbo owner and pending raised amount. No shares need to be burned for a yield-only claim.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged and accepted. Our intended lifecycle requires an updated, nonzero turbo-tranche NAV before processing yield-only claims. We accept the remaining limitation that yield-only claims revert when both NAV and claimable principal are zero. No code change planned.

issues.title: EIP-7702 delegation lets a malicious operator exceed the Bookbuild target
issues.body:
A malicious Bookbuild operator can use EIP-7702 to delegate its EOA to contract code that implements an ERC-1155 receiver callback. Because the delegated code executes in the operator account's context, it retains the same address and `OPERATOR_ROLE`. When Bookbuild shares are minted to the operator, the callback can reenter `processBids()` and cause the round to allocate more than its approved target.

#### Technical Details

`processBids()` copies the remaining target into memory and does not write the reduced value back to storage until after `DealVault.stakeFor()` returns. However, `stakeFor()` mints ERC-1155 shares to the winning bidder, which invokes the receiver callback before the reduced target is saved.

If the winning bidder is the operator's delegated EOA, the receiver callback can call `processBids()` again. The reentrant call passes `onlyOperator`, reads the original target from storage, and allocates another bid. When the outer call resumes, it completes using its stale in-memory target. Both bids can therefore be allocated even though only one fits within the approved raise.

#### Impact

The malicious operator can force a bidder who should have received a refund into an illiquid DealVault position and make the vault raise more capital than approved. The behavior requires deliberate abuse by the trusted Bookbuild operator and does not demonstrate theft or insolvency, so it is reported as Informational.

#### Recommendation

Make `processBids()` non-reentrant.

#### Developer Response


Acknowledged and accepted. No code change planned.

issues.title: Outstanding reservations can capture previously accrued yield
issues.body:
A user with an outstanding bookbuild reservation can exercise it immediately before a pending yield distribution and receive part of the yield that accrued before their shares existed.

#### Technical Details


`DealVaultBookbuild.takeReservation()` has no expiry, issuance epoch, or yield record-date restriction. It calls `DealVault.stakeFor()`, which accounts the recipient at the current interest index and mints their shares. A subsequent `DealVault.updateYield()` distributes the pending yield across the now-enlarged total supply:

```solidity
td.updateAccounting(_user, balanceOf(_user, _trancheId));
_mint(_user, _trancheId, shares, "");

// Later, in updateYield()
td.distributeInterests(_yield);
```

Consequently, a reservation holder can observe an `updateYield()` transaction, front-run it with `takeReservation()`, and immediately claim their pro-rata share of that distribution. A proof of concept demonstrates that when the incumbent and newly issued positions are equal, the new investor captures half of the pending yield.

#### Impact

Informational. Although the behaviour is exploitable, both its likelihood and practical impact are very low because it requires a pre-existing reservation and favourable transaction ordering, while the attacker’s principal remains invested.

#### Recommendation

Monitor reservation executions around yield distributions, particularly cases where a user enters immediately before updateYield() and claims shortly afterwards.

#### Developer Response

Acknowledged and accepted. The exploit is valid but unlikely. Reservation will be for partners and its usage will be agreed with involved parties.

issues.title: Partial-fill rounding can consume bids without transferring shares
Outstanding reservations can strand deposits after amortisation begins
issues.body:
An outstanding reservation can be exercised at any point while a DealVault is `ACTIVE`. A reservation holder can exercise it immediately before the vault moves to `AMORTISING`, leaving the new deposit permanently stranded in the vault.

#### Technical Details

`takeReservation()` has no deadline and remains available while the DealVault is `ACTIVE`. Exercising a reservation transfers the user's funds into the DealVault and adds them to `trancheAmountRaised`.

Only `start()` and `reraise()` sweep `trancheAmountRaised` to the deal receiver. Once `setToAmortising()` changes the vault state, `reraise()` is no longer available. `finalize()` distributes separately returned capital but does not sweep or refund the unsent raised amount. The reservation deposit therefore remains in the DealVault without a path for the user or existing holders to claim it.

#### Impact

The full amount deposited through the late reservation can become permanently inaccessible. The path is confined to one DealVault and requires a pre-existing reservation to be exercised immediately before amortisation, which makes occurrence rare. The permanent loss of a potentially material deposit supports Medium severity.

#### Recommendation

Add a deadline to each reservation and reject `takeReservation()` after it expires. As a backstop, have `setToAmortising()` iterate through the tranches and revert if any tranche has a raised amount greater than zero.

#### Developer Response

Mitigated in [PR #320](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/pull/320), commit [48809957](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/48809957b9ee53623952f5ada27414c751fa0ae7). Reservations expire seven days after being set and must be renewed to remain usable. `setToAmortising()` also rejects transitions while any supported token/tranche has unsent raised capital. Regression tests cover reservation expiry and amortisation after a reservation deposit.

issues.title: Remove the unused `NAV_PENDING` state
issues.body:
`EngineState` includes `NAV_PENDING`, but no code path uses it. The team confirmed that the state is unused and should be removed.

#### Recommendation

Remove `NAV_PENDING` and its unused references.

#### Developer Response

Addressed in [PR #320](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/pull/320), commit [30c9e308](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/30c9e308ca6871a3e5036c5878c7e5df187ae218). The unused `NAV_PENDING` enum member has been removed. `EngineState` now contains `NULL`, `PRE_WINDOW` and `SETTLING`; consequently, `SETTLING` has ordinal 2.

issues.title: Harden deployment and vault-creation validation
issues.body:
The deployment and vault-creation tooling omits several configuration checks and finalization steps. These can be addressed before transactions are submitted.

#### Bookbuild rounding buffer

The Bookbuild deployment does not fund the raise-token buffer expected by the ERC-4626 rounding remediation.

Transfer the intended buffer to `DealVaultBookbuild` during deployment and verify its balance afterward.

#### Duplicate DealVault currencies

`DealVaultFactory.createVault()` accepts duplicate currency addresses. A duplicate can cause the same currency balance to be counted more than once.

Add a uniqueness check to the script or backend that prepares each vault-creation transaction. For example:

```solidity
error DuplicateToken(address token);

function _validateUniqueTokens(address[] memory tokens_) internal pure {
    for (uint256 i; i < tokens_.length; ++i) {
        for (uint256 j; j < i; ++j) {
            if (tokens_[i] == tokens_[j]) {
                revert DuplicateToken(tokens_[i]);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Run `_validateUniqueTokens(tokens)` before submitting the `createVault()` transaction. When executed as local script or backend validation, this check is not part of the on-chain transaction and adds no gas cost. It provides an inexpensive safeguard against accidental misconfiguration.

#### FundingVault authority handoff

The deployment transfers ownership of the other principal contracts but leaves the canonical `FundingVault` owned by the deployer. The deployer also retains its temporary `OPERATOR_ROLE`.

After configuration is complete:

1. Transfer the canonical `FundingVault` to the intended timelock or multisig.
2. Revoke the deployer’s temporary `OPERATOR_ROLE`.
3. Verify the final owner, the intended operator assignment, and the absence of deployer authority.

#### Missing commit operator

The deployment does not grant `COMMIT_OPERATOR_ROLE`, which is required to use `commitFor()`.

Grant the role to the intended account during deployment and verify the assignment. If sponsored commits are intentionally disabled, document that decision and omit the role deliberately.

#### Recommendation

Implement the deployment, validation, and post-deployment checks described above.

#### Developer Response

Mitigated in [PR #320](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/pull/320), commit [333e6665](https://github.com/tenka-fi/10k/commit/333e6665599c80d77dfc324b63c3800abe636b1c). Each raise/re-raise now transfers 100,000 raw units of the raise token from the strategic operator into Bookbuild, funding the buffer when a round opens rather than at deployment.

The factory rejects duplicate currencies, and the mainnet script asserts final ownership, removal of deployer roles, and retention of the intended FundingVault operator. Regression tests cover buffer transfers and duplicate tokens. `COMMIT_OPERATOR_ROLE` remains deliberately unassigned because sponsored commits are not currently enabled.

issues.title: ERC-1155 callback gas griefing can block Bookbuild processing
issues.body:
A KYC-approved contract bidder can consume nearly all gas during its ERC-1155 receipt callback while still returning the correct acceptance value. This causes the outer Bookbuild processing transaction to run out of gas and revert, leaving the same hostile bid at the front of the queue on every retry.

#### Technical Details

`DealVaultBookbuild.processBids()` processes the highest-priority bid and calls `DealVault.stakeFor()` inside `try/catch`. Minting the bidder's DealVault shares invokes `onERC1155Received()` with nearly all remaining gas.

If the receiver consumes that gas and then returns successfully, `stakeFor()` succeeds and the existing failure-handling branch does not run. The Bookbuild subsequently runs out of gas before it can finish the batch and persist its progress. The entire transaction rolls back, restoring the hostile bid as the mandatory queue head. Retrying or processing a smaller batch cannot skip it.

#### Impact

The attacker can block allocation for every later bidder in the affected funded round. The attacker earns nothing and must commit capital through a KYC-approved address. Administrators can restore processing by revoking the bidder's KYC and retrying, so the issue is classified as Low.

#### Recommendation

Forward a fixed, tested amount of gas to `stakeFor()`. If the call exceeds that limit, use the existing failure path to remove the bid, transfer its recovered assets to Recovery, and continue processing the round.

#### Developer Response


Acknowledged and accepted. Extremely unlikely and can burn KYC nft if ever needed
